article.title: Why a Successful A/B Test May Still Be Too Small to Matter Financially
article.why: Practical English for customer analytics and business decisions.

paragraphs.en:
An A/B test can produce a statistically significant result and still be a poor business decision. Statistical significance asks whether the observed difference is difficult to explain by random sampling variation. It does not tell us whether the effect is large enough to pay for the campaign.

Consider a message that increases conversion from 1.00 percent to 1.05 percent in a very large experiment. With enough observations, the 0.05 percentage-point difference may be statistically convincing. But the absolute uplift is only five additional conversions per ten thousand contacted customers.

Financial evaluation starts by translating the effect into incremental volume. If one million customers are treated, a 0.05 percentage-point uplift implies about 500 additional conversions, assuming the estimate applies to that population.

Next comes contribution margin. If each incremental conversion contributes 2,000 yen, the gross incremental contribution is about one million yen. A campaign that costs three million yen to deliver would destroy value despite a statistically significant conversion lift.

Costs should include more than media spend. Discounts, points, call-center time, creative production, fulfillment, system operation, and opportunity cost can all matter. Some treatments also cannibalize full-price purchases that would have occurred without the offer.

Confidence intervals remain important. A point estimate may suggest positive profit while the plausible range includes economically unattractive outcomes. Decision makers should examine uncertainty around the business metric, not only the p-value for conversion.

Scale can work in both directions. A tiny per-customer effect may be valuable when treatment cost is near zero and the reachable population is enormous. Conversely, a large percentage uplift in a very small segment may create little total value.

Guardrails also matter. A campaign can improve short-term conversion while increasing unsubscribe, complaints, discount dependence, or returns. These effects should be included when they have meaningful economic consequences.

Pre-experiment planning should define both statistical and economic success criteria. A minimum detectable effect is a power concept; a minimum economically worthwhile effect is a business concept. They should be related but not confused.

After the test, report the control rate, treatment rate, absolute uplift, relative uplift, confidence interval, incremental customers, incremental margin, campaign cost, and ROI. This makes the decision transparent.

Where possible, evaluate persistence. An offer that shifts purchases forward by one week may show an immediate conversion gain without increasing longer-term demand. A follow-up window can reveal pull-forward effects.

Statistical evidence protects against mistaking noise for signal. Economic evaluation protects against investing in signals that are real but too small, too costly, or too temporary to matter.

Analysts should state the comparison population, observation window, and operational definition clearly so that the result can be reproduced. A useful business interpretation connects the metric to a mechanism, an action, and an economic consequence rather than treating the number as an isolated target.

Teams should also compare the result across meaningful customer segments. An aggregate improvement can hide deterioration in a strategically important group, while a weak overall result can conceal a valuable response in a smaller segment.

Operational feasibility belongs in the analysis. A theoretically attractive action creates little value if the data arrives too late, the channel lacks capacity, or the rule cannot be implemented consistently.

Finally, monitoring should continue after launch. Customer behavior, economics, and operational constraints can change, so the decision rule should be reviewed against current evidence rather than treated as permanent.
